reading.title: Counting in Prefixes
reading.purpose: Use number prefixes to work out the meaning of long, unfamiliar words.
paras: Many English words begin with a small piece that tells you a number. Learn these pieces and you can often guess the meaning of a long word you have never seen. Start with uni- and mono-, which both come from words for "one." Then add bi-, which means "two," tri-, which means "three," and multi-, which means "many."

Words with uni- and mono- often describe something done or held by one person or one group. A unilateral decision is made by one side without asking the others. A monopoly is control of a product by a single company, with no competitor. A monologue is a long speech by one person. Unanimous comes from Latin words meaning "one mind," so a unanimous vote means everyone agrees. In daily life, monotonous describes a task or sound that never changes, as if the world had only one note.

Bi- words involve two. A bilateral agreement is one that two countries, or two groups, make with each other. A bipartisan bill, in a country like the United States, has support from members of both major political parties. The prefix tri- gives us trilogy, a set of three works that tell one connected story. The ancient Greek playwright Aeschylus wrote one of the earliest known trilogies, three plays that follow one family.

Multi- is the prefix of large numbers. A multitude is a very large crowd, whether it is made of people or of birds. Something multifaceted has many sides, like a cut gem, and the word facet itself names one of those flat surfaces. A person can be multifaceted too. A student who plays the cello, builds robots, and writes poems has many sides to show. When a long word seems scary, cut it at the prefix and count. You will often find the number hiding at the start.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "monopoly" most nearly means
choices: a long speech that is given by only one person on a stage
a decision that is made by two sides who sit down together
control of a product by one company with no rival
a vote in which every member of the group agrees
qs.why: The text defines it directly: a monopoly is "control of a product by a single company, with no competitor."

choices: A bilateral agreement is one that two countries, or two groups, make with each other.
The prefix tri- gives us trilogy, a set of three works that tell one connected story.
A bipartisan bill, in a country like the United States, has support from members of both major political parties.
qs.why: Only this sentence names the word and explains that support comes from both major political parties.

ev.text: A bipartisan bill, in a country like the United States, has support from members of both major political parties.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Number prefixes help readers work out the meaning of long, unfamiliar words.
Words that begin with the same letters always have the same meaning in a sentence.
The Greeks invented every English word that begins with a prefix about numbers.
Most long words are too complicated to learn unless a reader studies Latin first.
qs.why: Each paragraph pairs a number prefix with words built from it, and the last one tells readers to cut a long word at the prefix and count.

qs.q: All twelve members of a club raise their hands for the same plan. Which word from the reading describes this vote?
qs.why: The reading says a unanimous vote means everyone agrees, which is exactly what happens when all twelve members vote the same way.
